herodotus.name: Herodotus
herodotus.summary: Greek historian and geographer (c. 484–c. 425 BC), called 'the Father of History' for his Histories, a detailed account of the Greco-Persian Wars and the peoples and lands around them.

isis.name: Isis
isis.summary: A major ancient Egyptian goddess, first recorded in the Old Kingdom, who resurrected her husband Osiris and protected their son Horus; her worship later spread across the Greco-Roman world.

ramesses-iv.name: Ramesses IV
ramesses-iv.summary: Third pharaoh of Egypt's Twentieth Dynasty, who became crown prince after his elder brother's death and ruled about six and a half years from around 1155 BC.

ramessesnakht.name: Ramessesnakht
ramessesnakht.summary: High Priest of Amun at Thebes during Egypt's Twentieth Dynasty, appointed under Ramesses IV and serving until Ramesses IX, as priestly power grew while the pharaoh's power declined.

high-priest-of-amun.name: High Priest of Amun
high-priest-of-amun.summary: The highest-ranking priest in the cult of the Egyptian god Amun, a role first appearing in the New Kingdom at the start of the Eighteenth Dynasty.

precinct-of-amun-re.name: Temple of Amun
precinct-of-amun-re.summary: The principal structure within the vast Precinct of Amun-Re at the Karnak Temple Complex near Luxor, Egypt, an enclosure of about 25 hectares dedicated to the god Amun-Re.

set-deity.name: Set (Seth)
set-deity.summary: Ancient Egyptian god of deserts, storms, disorder and foreigners, shown both as a protector who fought the serpent of chaos and as the murderer of his brother Osiris.

fayum-mummy-portraits.name: Fayum mummy portraits
fayum-mummy-portraits.summary: Naturalistic painted portraits attached to upper-class mummies in Roman-era Egypt, mostly from the Faiyum Basin, and the only large surviving body of classical panel painting.

kingdom-of-kush.name: Kingdom of Kush
kingdom-of-kush.summary: An ancient kingdom in Nubia along the Nile in what is now Sudan and Egypt, rising from the city-state of Kerma and later ruling Egypt itself in the 8th century BCE under King Piye.

new-kingdom-of-egypt.name: New Kingdom of Egypt
new-kingdom-of-egypt.summary: The period of ancient Egypt from about the 16th to 11th century BC, covering the 18th to 20th dynasties, marking Egypt's greatest power and territorial extent.

panel-painting.name: Panel painting
panel-painting.summary: Painting done on a flat wooden panel, the standard method besides frescoes and vellum before canvas became popular in the 16th century.

el-kurru.name: El-Kurru
el-kurru.summary: One of three royal cemeteries of the Kushite kings of Napata, Egypt's 25th Dynasty, in Sudan, used from about 860 to 650 BCE and home to Nubian pyramids.

piye.name: Piye
piye.summary: A Kushite king who founded Egypt's Twenty-fifth Dynasty, ruling 744–714 BC from the Nubian city of Napata.

shabaka.name: Shabaka
shabaka.summary: Third Kushite pharaoh of Egypt's Twenty-fifth Dynasty, reigning from 705 to 690 BC and ruling from the Nubian city of Napata.

shebitku.name: Shebitku
shebitku.summary: Second pharaoh of Egypt's Kushite 25th Dynasty, ruling from 714 to 705 BCE as son of the dynasty's founder Piye.

tantamani.name: Tantamani
tantamani.summary: Ruler of the Kingdom of Kush and the last pharaoh of Egypt's Twenty-fifth Dynasty, who died in 653 BC.

napata.name: Napata
napata.summary: An ancient city of Kush near the Nile's fourth cataract, home to a major Amun cult centre and sometime capital of the Kushite kingdom before Meroë took over in 593 BC.

mero.name: Meroë
mero.summary: An ancient city on the Nile in Sudan, capital of the Kingdom of Kush from around 590 BC until its collapse in the 4th century AD.

catacombs-of-kom-el-shoqafa.name: Catacombs of Kom El Shoqafa
catacombs-of-kom-el-shoqafa.summary: An Alexandria necropolis blending Egyptian, Greek and Roman styles, tunneled into bedrock in the 2nd century CE and rediscovered in 1900.

stele-of-piye.name: Stele of Piye
stele-of-piye.summary: An ancient Nubian monument, found at Jebel Barkal and now in Cairo's Egyptian Museum, recording King Piye's victory over Prince Tefnakht of Sais and his allies.

jebel-barkal.name: Jebel Barkal
jebel-barkal.summary: A flat-topped mesa near the Nile in Nubia, Sudan, with religious significance for both ancient Kush and ancient Egypt; a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2003.

red-monastery.name: Red Monastery
red-monastery.summary: A Coptic Orthodox monastery near Sohag in Upper Egypt, named for its red brick walls and built in a style similar to the nearby White Monastery.

white-monastery.name: White Monastery
white-monastery.summary: A Coptic Orthodox monastery near Sohag in Upper Egypt named for Saint Shenoute, once home to one of the largest Coptic libraries known.

sohag.name: Sohag
sohag.summary: A city on the west bank of the Nile in Egypt, capital of Sohag Governorate since 1960, near early Christian monasteries founded in the 4th century.

kharga-oasis.name: Kharga Oasis
kharga-oasis.summary: The southernmost of Egypt's five western oases, about 200 km west of the Nile valley and known to ancient Egyptians as the 'Southern Oasis.'

arqamani.name: Arqamani
arqamani.summary: Kushite king of Meroë who ruled from the late 3rd to early 2nd century BCE.

ptolemy-iv-philopator.name: Ptolemy IV Philopator
ptolemy-iv-philopator.summary: Fourth pharaoh of Ptolemaic Egypt, ruling 221 to 204 BC; his reign saw victory over the Seleucids at Raphia but is generally seen as marking the start of the dynasty's decline, amid criticism that he favored luxury over governing.

philae-temple-complex.name: Philae
philae-temple-complex.summary: An island-based temple complex on the Nile near Aswan, Egypt, dismantled and relocated in the 1960s–70s to save it from flooding by the new Aswan Dam.

ptolemy-v-epiphanes.name: Ptolemy V Epiphanes
ptolemy-v-epiphanes.summary: Pharaoh of Ptolemaic Egypt from 204 to 180 BC who inherited the throne at age five; his coronation in 196 BC as an adult ruler was commemorated by the creation of the Rosetta Stone.

ramesses-iii.name: Ramesses III
ramesses-iii.summary: Second pharaoh of Egypt's Twentieth Dynasty, reigning roughly 1185 to 1154 BC; the last New Kingdom pharaoh with real power, he defeated the Sea Peoples but was later assassinated in a harem conspiracy.

battle-of-djahy.name: Battle of Djahy
battle-of-djahy.summary: A land battle around 1178 BC in which Pharaoh Ramesses III's Egyptian forces defeated the invading Sea Peoples on Egypt's eastern frontier, known mainly from inscriptions at his mortuary temple.

battle-of-the-delta.name: Battle of the Delta
battle-of-the-delta.summary: A sea battle around 1175 BCE in which Pharaoh Ramesses III repelled a major Sea Peoples invasion near the Nile Delta, recorded on his mortuary temple walls at Medinet Habu.

sea-peoples.name: Sea Peoples
sea-peoples.summary: A group of tribes who raided Egypt and other eastern Mediterranean regions around 1200 BC, once seen as a main cause of the Bronze Age collapse but now often viewed as refugees fleeing an ongoing crisis.

ta-seti.name: Ta-Seti
ta-seti.summary: The first nome of Upper Egypt, on the border with Nubia, closely tied to early Nubian culture and sometimes used to name the Nubian region itself.

kerma-culture.name: Kerma culture
kerma-culture.summary: An early civilization and kingdom in ancient Nubia, in what is now Sudan, flourishing from about 2500 to 1500 BCE and rivaling Egypt before Egypt's New Kingdom absorbed it.

merneptah.name: Merneptah
merneptah.summary: Fourth pharaoh of Egypt's Nineteenth Dynasty, reigning for almost ten years from 1213 BC; son of Ramesses II, best known for the stele mentioning Israel.

marmarica.name: Marmarica
marmarica.summary: Ancient coastal region of Libya between Cyrenaica and Egypt, roughly corresponding to today's Libya–Egypt border area and including the Siwa Oasis.

libu.name: Libu
libu.summary: An ancient Libyan tribe of Berber origin, first recorded in Egyptian sources under Ramesses II and Merneptah in the 13th century BC, from whose name "Libya" derives.

meshwesh.name: Meshwesh
meshwesh.summary: An ancient Libyan tribe first recorded under pharaoh Amenhotep III around 1390-1350 BC, later often at war with Egypt and eventually ruling it during the 22nd and 23rd Dynasties.

esarhaddon.name: Esarhaddon
esarhaddon.summary: King of the Neo-Assyrian Empire (681–669 BCE), famous for conquering Egypt in 671 BCE and for rebuilding Babylon after his father had destroyed it.

taharqa.name: Taharqa
taharqa.summary: A pharaoh of Egypt's Twenty-fifth Dynasty and king of Kush who ruled from 690 to 664 BC, one of the Nubian rulers known as the Black Pharaohs.

medinet-habu.name: Medinet Habu
medinet-habu.summary: An archaeological site near Luxor, Egypt, centred on the mortuary temple of Ramesses III, known for reliefs depicting the pharaoh's victory over the Sea Peoples around 1186 to 1155 BCE.

ashurbanipal.name: Ashurbanipal
ashurbanipal.summary: King of the Neo-Assyrian Empire from 669 to 631 BC, often called the last great Assyrian king, whose 38-year reign marked both the empire's height and the start of its decline.

harran.name: Harran
harran.summary: Ancient city in Upper Mesopotamia, founded between the 25th and 20th centuries BC, a major religious centre devoted to the moon god Sin and site of the 53 BC Battle of Carrhae.

amasis-ii.name: Amasis II
amasis-ii.summary: Pharaoh of Egypt's Twenty-sixth Dynasty who reigned 570 to 526 BCE, the last great ruler before the Persian conquest and the first pharaoh to conquer Cyprus since Thutmose III.

nebuchadnezzar-ii.name: Nebuchadnezzar II
nebuchadnezzar-ii.summary: Second king of the Neo-Babylonian Empire, ruling 605 to 562 BC; renowned for military victories including Carchemish and for major construction projects in Babylon.

hakor.name: Hakor
hakor.summary: An ancient Egyptian pharaoh of the 29th Dynasty whose 13-year reign — more than half the dynasty's entire span — marked its high point.

twenty-ninth-dynasty-of-egypt.name: Twenty-Ninth Dynasty
twenty-ninth-dynasty-of-egypt.summary: A short-lived Egyptian dynasty founded by Nefaarud I in 398 BCE after overthrowing Amyrtaeus, ending in 380 BCE with the overthrow of Nefaarud II.

ramesses-v.name: Ramesses V
ramesses-v.summary: Fourth pharaoh of Egypt's Twentieth Dynasty and son of Ramesses IV; his mummy is now displayed at the National Museum of Egyptian Civilization in Cairo.

deir-el-medina.name: Set Maat
deir-el-medina.summary: The ancient Egyptian name for Deir el-Medina, meaning 'Place of Truth,' a workmen's village housing the artisans who built royal tombs in the Valley of the Kings, 1550-1080 BC.

kv9.name: KV9
kv9.summary: Tomb in Egypt's Valley of the Kings built for Pharaoh Ramesses V and later reused by Ramesses VI; work on it helped keep the nearby tomb of Tutankhamun hidden.

meroitic-script.name: Meroitic script
meroitic-script.summary: Two related scripts, cursive and hieroglyphic, developed to write the Meroitic language of the Kingdom of Kush from the 3rd century BC, used into the 5th century AD.

coptic-script.name: Coptic script
coptic-script.summary: The writing system used for the Coptic language, based on the Greek alphabet with extra letters borrowed from Egyptian Demotic script, the first alphabetic script for Egyptian.

story-of-wenamun.name: The Story of Wenamun
story-of-wenamun.summary: An ancient Egyptian literary text about a noble robbed while traveling to buy cedar, known from a single incomplete papyrus copy found in 1890.

septuagint.name: Septuagint
septuagint.summary: The earliest surviving Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible, made by Jews in the Ptolemaic Kingdom, mainly around Alexandria, from the 3rd to 2nd century BC.

callimachus.name: Callimachus of Libya
callimachus.summary: An ancient Greek poet and scholar from Cyrene, in modern-day Libya, active at the Library of Alexandria in the 3rd century BC, where he catalogued Greek literature.

theocritus.name: Theocritus of Syracuse
theocritus.summary: Greek poet from Sicily, born around 300 BC, credited as the creator of ancient pastoral poetry.

nonnus.name: Nonnus of Panopolis
nonnus.summary: A Greek epic poet of the Imperial Roman era, probably active in the 5th century AD, from Panopolis in Egypt, best known for the epic Dionysiaca about the god Dionysus.

dionysiaca.name: Dionysiaca
dionysiaca.summary: An epic poem by the 5th-century AD poet Nonnus, the longest surviving poem from Greco-Roman antiquity, centered on the god Dionysus's expedition to India.

manetho.name: Manetho
manetho.summary: An Egyptian priest under the Ptolemaic Kingdom (fl. 290–260 BCE) who wrote the Aegyptiaca, a Greek history of Egypt organizing its rulers into the dynasties still used today.

ptolemy-ii-philadelphus.name: Ptolemy II Philadelphus
ptolemy-ii-philadelphus.summary: Son of Ptolemy I who ruled Egypt from 284 to 246 BC, presiding over the height of Alexandria's cultural splendor and the growth of its Museum and Library, while waging costly wars to expand Ptolemaic territory.

aegyptiaca.name: Aegyptiaca
aegyptiaca.summary: Greek-language history of ancient Egypt written by the priest Manetho around 290–260 BCE, organizing Egyptian rulers into thirty-one dynasties.

corpus-hermeticum.name: Corpus Hermeticum
corpus-hermeticum.summary: A collection of 17 Greek texts (written c. 100-300 CE) attributed to the legendary Hermes Trismegistus, later translated into Latin in the 1400s and hugely influential on Renaissance thought.

hermes-trismegistus.name: Hermes Trismegistus
hermes-trismegistus.summary: Legendary Hellenistic figure combining the Greek god Hermes and Egyptian god Thoth, regarded as author of the Hermetica writings underlying Hermeticism.

ramesses-ii.name: Ramesses II
ramesses-ii.summary: Third pharaoh of Egypt's Nineteenth Dynasty (c. 1303–1213 BC), often called Ramesses the Great; his 66-year reign, the longest of any pharaoh, included 15 military campaigns.

thebaid.name: Thebaid
thebaid.summary: A region of ancient Egypt made up of the 13 southernmost nomes of Upper Egypt, stretching from Abydos to Aswan.

diodorus-siculus.name: Diodorus Siculus
diodorus-siculus.summary: Ancient Greek historian from Sicily (1st century BC) who wrote the 40-book universal history Bibliotheca historica, covering world history up to about 60 BC.

percy-bysshe-shelley.name: Percy Bysshe Shelley
percy-bysshe-shelley.summary: An English Romantic poet (1792–1822), little recognized in his lifetime but hugely influential afterward, known for works such as 'Ozymandias' and 'Ode to the West Wind'.

ozymandias.name: Ozymandias
ozymandias.summary: A sonnet by English Romantic poet Percy Bysshe Shelley, first published in 1818, about the ruined legacy of a great Egyptian pharaoh.

alexander-the-great.name: Alexander the Great
alexander-the-great.summary: King of Macedon from 336 BC who conquered much of the known world by age 30, creating an empire stretching from Greece to India; tutored by Aristotle.

ptolemy.name: Ptolemy
ptolemy.summary: A Greco-Roman scholar of the 2nd century AD who wrote influential works on astronomy, geography and astrology; his geocentric model of the universe, promoted by the Catholic Church, was studied for over a thousand years.

sostratus-of-cnidus.name: Sostratus of Cnidus
sostratus-of-cnidus.summary: A Greek architect and engineer of the 3rd century BC, said to have designed the Lighthouse of Alexandria around 280 BC, though this claim is disputed.

ptolemy-i-soter.name: Ptolemy I Soter
ptolemy-i-soter.summary: A Macedonian Greek general and companion of Alexander the Great who became pharaoh of Egypt from 305/304 BC, founding the Ptolemaic dynasty and commissioning the Library and Lighthouse of Alexandria.

eratosthenes.name: Eratosthenes
eratosthenes.summary: Ancient Greek polymath (c. 276–c. 195 BC) and chief librarian at Alexandria, first known to calculate Earth's circumference and axial tilt, and founder of scientific chronology and geography as a field.

saqiyah.name: Saqiyah
saqiyah.summary: A mechanical water-lifting device, also called a Persian wheel, turned by animal power to raise water via buckets on a vertical wheel, used mainly for irrigation.

faiyum.name: Faiyum
faiyum.summary: A city in Egypt's Faiyum Oasis, about 100 kilometres southwest of Cairo, and one of the country's oldest cities owing to its strategic location.

herophilos.name: Herophilos
herophilos.summary: Greek physician (335–280 BC) regarded as one of the earliest anatomists and often called the father of anatomy for systematically dissecting human cadavers and recording his findings.

erasistratus.name: Erasistratus
erasistratus.summary: Greek anatomist and royal physician (c. 304–c. 250 BC) who, with Herophilus, founded a school of anatomy in Alexandria and performed early dissections, seen as a potential founder of neuroscience.

ptolemaic-dynasty.name: Ptolemaic dynasty
ptolemaic-dynasty.summary: The Macedonian Greek royal family that ruled Egypt from Alexandria for 275 years, from 305 BC until Rome's annexation in 30 BC, founding the Library of Alexandria and blending Greek and Egyptian traditions.

almagest.name: Almagest
almagest.summary: Ptolemy's 2nd-century astronomical treatise that established the geocentric model of the universe, accepted for over 1,200 years.

tetrabiblos.name: Tetrabiblos
tetrabiblos.summary: A 2nd-century text on astrology by the Alexandrian scholar Claudius Ptolemy, a companion to his astronomical work the Almagest and long an authoritative work on the subject.

handy-tables.name: Handy Tables
handy-tables.summary: A set of astronomical tables the 2nd-century astronomer Ptolemy compiled after the Almagest, simplified for practical use and influential through late antiquity and medieval times.

necho-ii.name: Necho II
necho-ii.summary: A pharaoh of Egypt's 26th Dynasty (610–595 BC) whose fleet reportedly sailed around Africa, and who killed King Josiah of Judah before losing a war with Babylon.

callixenus-of-rhodes.name: Callixenus of Rhodes
callixenus-of-rhodes.summary: A Hellenistic author from Rhodes, contemporary with several Ptolemaic kings of Egypt; he wrote two works, both now lost.

john-peter-oleson.name: John Peter Oleson
john-peter-oleson.summary: Canadian classical archaeologist and historian (born 1946) specializing in Roman technology, including water-lifting devices and Roman concrete construction.

noria.name: Noria
noria.summary: A hydropowered scoop wheel used to lift water into an aqueduct, for irrigation or to supply water to cities and villages.

coptic-language.name: Coptic language
coptic-language.summary: The last stage of the Egyptian language, spoken from the 3rd century AD and written in the Coptic alphabet; replaced by Arabic but still used in church liturgy.

twenty-fifth-dynasty-of-egypt.name: Twenty-fifth Dynasty
twenty-fifth-dynasty-of-egypt.summary: Also called the Nubian or Kushite Dynasty, this line of pharaohs from the Kingdom of Kush ruled part or all of Egypt from 744 to 656 BCE, reuniting Egypt with Kush.

satrap.name: Satrap
satrap.summary: A provincial governor in the ancient Persian and later Hellenistic and Sasanian empires, acting as a semi-autonomous viceroy; the word later came to mean a corrupt or tyrannical local ruler.

basileus.name: Basileus
basileus.summary: A Greek title meaning king or emperor, used by ancient Greek rulers, Byzantine emperors and later kings of Greece; it is also the source of the name Basil.

cambyses-ii.name: Cambyses II
cambyses-ii.summary: Second king of the Achaemenid Persian Empire, ruling 530 to 522 BCE; son of Cyrus the Great, he conquered Egypt and Libya's coast before dying of a wound on his way home.

psamtik-iii.name: Psamtik III
psamtik-iii.summary: Last pharaoh of Egypt's Twenty-sixth Dynasty, ruling only six months in 526 to 525 BC before being defeated by Persia's Cambyses II at the Battle of Pelusium and later dying by suicide in captivity.

battle-of-pelusium.name: Battle of Pelusium
battle-of-pelusium.summary: A 525 BC battle near Egypt's Nile Delta in which Persia's Cambyses II defeated Pharaoh Psamtik III, transferring Egypt's throne to Persia and beginning its Twenty-seventh Dynasty.

twenty-sixth-dynasty-of-egypt.name: Twenty-sixth Dynasty (Saite Period)
twenty-sixth-dynasty-of-egypt.summary: Last native dynasty of ancient Egypt before the Persian conquest, ruling 664 to 525 BC from the city of Sais; its reign is also called the Saite Period.

psamtik-i.name: Psamtik I
psamtik-i.summary: First pharaoh of Egypt's Twenty-sixth Dynasty, ruling from Sais from 664 to 610 BCE; installed by the Assyrian king Ashurbanipal, he later gained more independence as Assyrian power declined.

thirtieth-dynasty-of-egypt.name: Thirtieth Dynasty
thirtieth-dynasty-of-egypt.summary: The last native royal dynasty of ancient Egypt, founded in 380 BCE by Nectanebo I and ended by the Persian invasion of 343 BCE.

nectanebo-ii.name: Nectanebo II
nectanebo-ii.summary: The last native pharaoh of ancient Egypt, ruling 358 to about 340 BC, until betrayal by his own servant let the Persians conquer Egypt.

twentieth-dynasty-of-egypt.name: Twentieth Dynasty
twentieth-dynasty-of-egypt.summary: The last dynasty of ancient Egypt's New Kingdom, ruling 1189–1077 BCE, whose reign is generally seen as the start of Egypt's decline amid invasions by the Sea Peoples.

perdiccas.name: Perdiccas
perdiccas.summary: A Macedonian general and bodyguard of Alexander the Great who became regent of his empire after his death, ruling from Babylon until his assassination in 320 BC.

wars-of-the-diadochi.name: Wars of the Diadochi
wars-of-the-diadochi.summary: The struggles among Alexander the Great's generals for control of his empire after his death in 323 BC, lasting until 272 BC and establishing the Ptolemaic and Seleucid dynasties.

tausret.name: Tausret
tausret.summary: Final pharaoh of Egypt's Nineteenth Dynasty, who died in 1188 BC; her independent reign lasted roughly two to three years after she assumed her predecessor Siptah's regnal years.

nineteenth-dynasty-of-egypt.name: 19th Dynasty
nineteenth-dynasty-of-egypt.summary: The second dynasty of Egypt's New Kingdom, lasting from 1292 to 1189 BC, founded by Ramesses I and part of what is called the Ramesside period.

setnakhte.name: Setnakhte
setnakhte.summary: First pharaoh of Egypt's Twentieth Dynasty, ruling 1188 to 1185 BC, and father of Ramesses III.

hezekiah.name: Hezekiah
hezekiah.summary: King of Judah from about 716 to 687 BCE, called the best-documented figure in biblical history for his religious reforms, revolt against Assyria, and extensive Assyrian and biblical records.

sennacherib.name: Sennacherib
sennacherib.summary: King of the Neo-Assyrian Empire from 705 to 681 BC, famed in the Hebrew Bible for his Levant campaign, who destroyed Babylon in 689 BC and expanded the capital Nineveh.

karnak.name: Karnak
karnak.summary: A vast temple complex near Luxor, Egypt, begun under Senusret I around 1971-1926 BC and expanded through the Ptolemaic period, serving as the main place of worship of the god Amun.

turin-king-list.name: Turin King List
turin-king-list.summary: An ancient Egyptian hieratic papyrus, likely from Ramesses II's reign, listing over 200 kings and serving as the main basis for Egyptian chronology before his time.

dag-herbj-rnsrud.name: Dag Herbjørnsrud
dag-herbj-rnsrud.summary: Norwegian historian of ideas, author and former editor-in-chief, and founder of a center for global and comparative history of ideas in Oslo, writing on decolonizing philosophy and global intellectual history.

isocrates.name: Isocrates
isocrates.summary: Ancient Greek rhetorician (436-338 BC) and one of the ten Attic orators, who wrote works urging the Greeks to unite against Persia and reportedly starved himself to death near age 100.

pythagoras.name: Pythagoras
pythagoras.summary: Ancient Greek philosopher and polymath (c. 570–495 BC) from Samos, founder of Pythagoreanism, later credited with the Pythagorean theorem and the doctrine of transmigration of souls.

edict-of-milan.name: Edict of Milan
edict-of-milan.summary: An agreement in 313 CE between Roman emperors Constantine I and Licinius to end persecution and grant Christians legal status, though Christianity became the empire's official religion only later, in 380.

origen.name: Origen
origen.summary: Early Christian theologian from Alexandria (c. 185 – c. 253) who wrote roughly 2,000 theological works and died of injuries suffered during the Decian persecution of 250.

clement-of-alexandria.name: Clement of Alexandria
clement-of-alexandria.summary: Christian theologian and philosopher (c. 147–215 AD) who taught in Alexandria and blended Christian thought with Greek philosophy, especially Plato and the Stoics.

phaedrus-dialogue.name: Phaedrus
phaedrus-dialogue.summary: A dialogue written by Plato around 370 BC, between Socrates and Phaedrus, discussing rhetoric, love, and the nature of the human soul.

thoth.name: Thoth
thoth.summary: An ancient Egyptian deity of the Moon, wisdom and writing, credited in mythology with inventing hieroglyphs and maintaining cosmic order alongside Ma'at.

plato.name: Plato
plato.summary: An ancient Greek philosopher (c. 428–347 BC) considered the foundational thinker of Western philosophy, who founded the Academy in Athens and developed the Theory of Forms.

serapis.name: Serapis
serapis.summary: A Graeco-Egyptian god formed by blending Osiris and Apis, promoted from the 3rd century BC by Ptolemy I Soter to unite his Greek and Egyptian subjects, and later popular across the Roman Empire.

osiris.name: Osiris
osiris.summary: Ancient Egyptian god of fertility, the afterlife and resurrection, killed by his brother Set and restored to life after his sister-wife Isis gathered his scattered remains.

apis-deity.name: Apis
apis-deity.summary: A sacred bull worshipped in ancient Egyptian religion, identified as Hathor's son and later an intermediary between humans and gods such as Ptah and Osiris.

desert-fathers.name: Desert Fathers
desert-fathers.summary: Early Christian hermits who settled in Egypt's Wadi El Natrun from around the third century; their example, especially Anthony the Great's, shaped the rise of Christian monasticism.

wadi-el-natrun.name: Wadi El Natrun
wadi-el-natrun.summary: A low-lying valley in northern Egypt, known in Christian tradition as Scetis, that became one of the earliest and most important centers of Christian monasticism.

skete.name: Skete
skete.summary: A monastic community in Eastern Christianity blending solitary and communal life, its name likely from the Scetis valley in Egypt where it originated.

timaeus-dialogue.name: Timaeus
timaeus-dialogue.summary: A dialogue written by Plato around 360 BC, featuring long speeches on the creation of the world, the World Soul, and the myth of Atlantis.

socrates.name: Socrates
socrates.summary: Ancient Greek philosopher from Athens (c. 470–399 BC), often called the first Western moral philosopher, known through his students Plato and Xenophon; sentenced to death for impiety.

solon.name: Solon
solon.summary: Athenian statesman, lawmaker and poet (c. 630–560 BCE), one of the Seven Sages of Greece, credited with reforms that laid the foundations of Athenian democracy.

aristotle.name: Aristotle
aristotle.summary: Ancient Greek philosopher and polymath (384–322 BC) who founded the Peripatetic school, tutored Alexander the Great, and laid groundwork for modern science.

politics-aristotle.name: Politics (Aristotle)
politics-aristotle.summary: A work of political philosophy by Aristotle exploring how people should best live together in communities, based partly on his research collecting 158 constitutions of Greek city-states.

horapollo.name: Horapollo
horapollo.summary: Supposed 5th-century author of Hieroglyphica, a treatise on Egyptian hieroglyphs known through a Greek translation.

histories-herodotus.name: Histories
histories-herodotus.summary: Herodotus's work from the 5th century BC, considered the founding text of history writing in the West, covering the rise of the Persian Empire and the Greco-Persian Wars.

aethiopia.name: Aethiopia
aethiopia.summary: A classical Greek term for dark-skinned peoples living south of Egypt and elsewhere, used by Homer and Herodotus; Byzantine Greeks later applied it to the Aksumites after their king conquered Meroë in 330 CE.

elephantine.name: Elephantine
elephantine.summary: An island on the Nile forming part of Aswan in Upper Egypt, known for Aramaic papyri documenting a Jewish mercenary community and its temple, destroyed in 410 BC.

mark-the-evangelist.name: Mark the Evangelist
mark-the-evangelist.summary: Early Christian traditionally credited as author of the Gospel of Mark and founder of the episcopal see of Alexandria; venerated as a saint with a feast day on April 25.

pope-demetrius-i-of-alexandria.name: Pope Demetrius I
pope-demetrius-i-of-alexandria.summary: 12th Bishop and Patriarch of Alexandria, who died in 232; ancient sources differ on the exact year his tenure began.

udjahorresnet.name: Udjahorresnet
udjahorresnet.summary: Ancient Egyptian high official active at the end of the 26th and start of the 27th Dynasty, known for promoting Egyptian customs to the early Achaemenid Persian kings.

justinian-i.name: Justinian I
justinian-i.summary: Roman emperor from 527 to 565 whose generals reconquered much of the former Western Roman Empire and who is remembered for his sweeping rewrite of Roman law.
